Non-explosion principles for branched rough differential equations with unbounded coefficients
Kexing Ying

Abstract
Expanding upon the work of [ LY25 ] , we provide a non-explosion criterion for branched rough differential equations (bRDEs) where we continue to allow for the drift and the rough coefficient to be unbounded in the branched setting. Moreover, by providing a characterization of “pure area” branched rough paths – branched rough paths over the zero path, we provide two different constructions of bRDEs which explode in finite time, and thus demonstrating the sharpness of the criterion. Finally, by realizing a trade-off between the growth of the coefficient of the bRDE and the decay of its higher-order derivatives, we provide a new non-explosion principle for bRDEs which allows for the coefficient to grow even faster than what is provided in [ LY25 ] .

†

The author would like to thank Xue-Mei Li for their supervision and helpful discussions.
The author acknowledges support from the Swiss National Science Foundation project MINT (10000849)
and from NCCR SwissMAP.

1
Introduction

The theory of rough paths, introduced in the seminal works of Lyons
[
Lyo94
,
Lyo98
]
, provides a path-wise framework for
differential equations driven by signals that are too irregular for classical calculus
(say having Hölder regularity
\gamma<\frac{1}{2}
).
It restores the convergence of the Riemann sum by enriching the driving signal with
an extra component corresponding to the second-order iterated integral.
This viewpoint was demonstrated to be an especially powerful tool in stochastic analysis as it
provides a deterministic formulation of equations driven by stochastic processes,
e.g. (fractional) Brownian motions. Moreover, it restores the continuity of the
solution map with respect to the driving signal and the component corresponding to the iterated integral.
We note the standard references on rough path theory
[
FV10
]
and
[
FH20
]
while we also
remark on some of its successful applications in multiscale systems (e.g.
[
CFK+19
,
HL22
,
GL21
,
LPSY25
]
),
(S)PDEs (e.g.
[
DOR15
,
DGHT19
,
HLN19
,
LS26
]
), and in the context of machine learning
(e.g.
[
CK26
,
KKA+19
,
MSKF21
]
) just to name a few.

For paths with Hölder regularity
\gamma<\frac{1}{3}
, extra care is needed and additional components are required to ensure the
convergence of the Riemann sum. In this case, the rough paths most commonly considered are the so-called
geometric rough paths, which are namely the rough paths whose integration theory
satisfies the usual chain rule and are enriched with components corresponding to the
higher-order iterated integrals. These rough paths arise naturally as limits of
smooth paths and are well-suited for many applications. Nevertheless, e.g. in the context of
finance, where Itô integration is preferred over Stratonovich for the payoff of a continuous-time strategy,
as the latter can be heuristically described as “seeing into the future”,
the geometric rough path formalism is not necessarily always desirable. The search for the correct notion
of rough paths in this setting led to the introduction of branched rough paths by Gubinelli in

[
Gub04
,
Gub06
]
(see also
[
CW16
]
in the infinite-dimensional case).
We also note the articles
[
TZ20
,
VRST25
]
which contain a nice overview of branched rough paths.
In this case, the components enriching the path no longer just correspond to the (linear) iterated integrals,
but also integrals of the products (of the integral of products, and so on). This is in contrast to the geometric case,
in which these components are simply reduced to the iterated integrals via the shuffle relations. Instead, in the
absence of the chain rule, these data are naturally encoded by the Hopf algebra of rooted trees
(namely the Connes-Kreimer Hopf algebra, cf.
[
Hof03
,
OG05
]
).

We in this article study non-explosion for rough differential equations (RDEs) driven by these branched
rough paths. More precisely, we consider branched rough differential equations (bRDEs) of the form

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:bRDE-intro}\differential\mathbf{Y}_{t}=b(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\,\differential t+\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\,\differential\mathbf{X}_{t},

(1.1)

where
\mathbf{X}
is a branched rough path and the coefficients are allowed to be unbounded.
For geometric RDEs, global existence of RDEs with unbounded coefficients
has been studied by many authors, including but not limited to the works of

[
Dav07
,
Bai12
,
Dri18
,
BC20
]
and also
[
RS17
]
in which the latter established
non-explosion of (
1.1
) assuming
b
having linear growth and
\varphi
bounded.
For RDEs driven by non-geometric rough paths in the
\gamma\in{\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}\right]}
regime,
we also note the works
[
Lej09
,
Lej
]
which showed non-explosion of the RDE while assuming
that the coefficient has bounded derivative. We also mention the works of
[
FIZ07
,
SS17
,
ALL23
,
Anz24
]

regarding strong completeness and path-by-path
well-posedness of SDEs which are closely related to the non-explosion problem for RDEs when the driving signal is the Itô rough path lift
of a Brownian motion. In the context of bRDEs, we note
[
BCMW22
]
in which the authors
studied the “coming down from infinity” property of a bRDE with a cubic drift
(albeit in this case, the drift has a damping effect rather than a growth effect).

The present work is mainly motivated by the work of Li with the author
[
LY25
]
and extends
the non-explosion principles presented there to the branched setting. In particular, we provide a
non-explosion criterion for bRDEs with drift for which we observe that a trade-off can be made
between the growth of the drift coefficient
b
and the growth of the rough coefficient
\varphi
.
Moreover, we obtain a new non-explosion principle for bRDEs by observing that a trade-off can be
made between the growth of the coefficient
\varphi
and the decay of its higher-order derivatives.
Finally, by providing a characterization of branched rough paths over the zero path, we provide
two different constructions of bRDEs which explode in finite time, demonstrating the sharpness of the non-explosion
criterion.

We remark that the non-explosion criterion we provide is independent of the choice of the rough
path lift. Thus, by transforming the higher order components of the branched rough path appropriately, one
might achieve a better growth condition than what is provided directly by the criterion. The example of comparing
the Stratonovich lift against the Itô lift of a Brownian motion already illustrates this as one
version could have a better growth condition than the other. Namely, the correction term could
provide cancellation or could worsen the growth condition. Consequently, while one can generally
write a bRDE as a geometric RDE on an extended space via the Hairer-Kelly embedding
[
HK14
]

(cf. also
[
BC19
]
),
the criterion one obtains after applying this embedding is most certainly not optimal.
More commentary on this phenomenon can also be observed in the examples of Section
5
.

Finally, we also note that working in the branched setting is also motivated by the similarities it bears
to analogous controlled-type descriptions used in the theory of singular SPDEs
[
Hai14
]
.
In those theories, the same Hopf algebra structure appears as a consequence of
the Picard iterations of Duhamel’s formula. We note the article
[
BCFP19
]

which provides a detailed analysis of the algebraic structure of branched rough paths and Hairer’s
theory of regularity structures. One example of interest is the recent work
[
GH26
]
,
in which the authors discussed “a pure area model”, i.e. a non-trivial lift over the trivial noise.
This is the analogue of the pure area rough path in the context of regularity structures and so,
one reasonably expects that the discussion in Section
5.1
on pure area branched rough paths
could be extended to this context. In this light, one may hope that the technique developed
here could be furthered to the setting of singular SPDEs, in which the non-explosion problem is of
even greater interest.

1.1
Strategy for non-explosion

We outline the strategy used to show non-explosion of an RDE.
For simplicity, in this section we assume that we work at level
N=2
and that the
rough differential equation has no drift, i.e. we consider
Y:[0,\xi)\to\mathbb{R}^{m}
the
maximal solution to the RDE

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:rde-strat}\differential Y_{t}=\varphi(Y_{t})\differential\mathbf{X}_{t},

(1.2)

where
\mathbf{X}\in{\mathcal{C}}^{\gamma}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{d})
is a
\gamma
-Hölder rough path with

\gamma\in(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}]
and
\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to{\mathcal{L}}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{m})
.

The proof strategy for showing non-explosion of
(Y_{t})
essentially boils down to the following simple
observation. Suppose
(r_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{+}
is a non-decreasing sequence such that

r_{n}\to\infty
as
n\to\infty
. We keep track of the location of
Y
by introducing the times

\tau^{r_{n}}=\tau^{n}=\inf\{t:\|Y_{t}\|\geq r_{n}\}
and
\sigma^{r_{n}}=\sigma^{n}=\sup\{t<\tau^{n+1}:\|Y_{t}\|\leq r_{n}\}

so that
\|Y_{t}\|\in[r_{n},r_{n+1}]
for all
t\in[\sigma^{n},\tau^{n+1})
. Then, for
any
t>0
, if

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:tau-ineq}\|Y_{(\sigma^{n}+t)\wedge\tau^{n+1}}-Y_{\sigma^{n}}\|<r_{n+1}-r_{n}

(1.3)

for some
n\in\mathbb{N}
, we have that
t<\tau^{n+1}-\sigma^{n}
.
Consequently, if we can find a sequence
(t_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
such that for each
n\in\mathbb{N}
,
Equation (
1.3
) holds for
t=t_{n}
, then

\xi=\lim_{n\to\infty}\tau^{n}\geq\sum_{n=N}^{\infty}(\tau^{{n+1}}-\tau^{n})\geq\sum_{n=N}^{\infty}(\tau^{n+1}-\sigma^{n})>\sum_{n=N}^{\infty}t_{n}.

Thus, we may conclude that the RDE has non-explosion if
(t_{n})
can be chosen to be non-summable.

A natural contender for the contour sequence
(r_{n})
is to take
r_{n}=Rn
for some constant

R>0
. In this case, denoting the integral
\int_{0}^{t}\varphi(Y_{s})\differential\mathbf{X}_{s}=:Z_{t}
, we may observe
the simple estimate

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:del-Y-est}\begin{split}\|Y_{(\sigma^{n}+t)\wedge\tau^{n+1}}-Y_{\sigma^{n}}\|&=\|Z_{(\sigma^{n}+t)\wedge\tau^{n+1}}-Z_{\sigma^{n}}\|\\
&\leq\|R^{Z}_{\sigma^{n},(\sigma^{n}+t)\wedge\tau^{n+1}}\|+\|\varphi(Y_{\sigma^{n}})\|\|X\|_{\gamma}t^{\gamma}\end{split}

(1.4)

with
R^{Z}_{s,t}:=Z_{t}-Z_{s}-\varphi(Y_{s})(X_{t}-X_{s})
, i.e. it is the remainder term in the
construction of the rough integral in the context of controlled rough paths.
Thus, assuming a sub-linear growth condition on
\varphi
of the form

\|\varphi(y)\|\lesssim\|y\|^{\gamma}
, by taking
t_{n}=\varepsilon n^{-1}
for some
small
\varepsilon
independent of
n
, the term
\|\varphi(Y_{\sigma^{n}})\|\|X\|_{\gamma}t^{\gamma}

can be made uniformly (in
n
) arbitrarily small. On the other hand, under certain conditions, it can be shown
that the Hölder norm of the remainder
R^{Z}
can be controlled on sufficiently small intervals
(cf. Corollary
4.6
). To be more precise, for
t<r_{n}^{-1}
, we have the estimate

\|R^{Z}_{\sigma^{n},(\sigma^{n}+t)\wedge\tau^{n+1}}\|\leq\|R^{Z}\|_{2\gamma;I}t^{2\gamma}\lesssim(R(n+1))^{2\gamma}t^{2\gamma}

where
I:=[\sigma^{n},(\sigma^{n}+t)\wedge\tau^{n+1}]
.
Hence, for
t_{n}
chosen above (shrinking
\varepsilon
if necessary),
the remainder term can also be made uniformly arbitrarily small. Thus, choosing
\varepsilon
so that
both terms are strictly less than
\frac{1}{2}R
provides the desired estimate.

In the presence of a drift, the above argument can be adapted (cf.
[
LY25
, Lemma 3.5 and Theorem 4.12]
)
and a similar conclusion holds for the solution of the RDE under the same growth conditions on
\varphi
.
To be
slightly
more precise, by an analogous argument, one can control the growth of the
solution of a perturbed ODE of the form

\differential Y_{t}=b(Y_{t})\differential t+\differential\gamma_{t}

provided one has sufficient control over the perturbation
\gamma
. With this, we can bootstrap
the previous control by considering instead the system

\begin{cases}\differential Y_{t}&=b(Y_{t})\differential t+\differential\eta_{t}\\
\differential\eta_{t}&=\varphi(Y_{t})\differential\mathbf{X}_{t}\end{cases}.

We in this article generalize this result to the setting of branched RDEs resulting in
Theorem
4.7
. For this, we provide an a priori estimates on the higher-order
Gubinelli derivatives of the solution in Section
3.2
from which we deduce the aforementioned
estimates on the remainder term
R^{Z}
in this lower regularity setting (Corollary
4.6
).
Moreover, in proving this remainder estimate, one quickly realizes that
the bound remains to hold while allowing
\varphi
to have faster growth should its derivatives
have sufficient decay. This naturally leads to the question of whether one can still show a similar
non-explosion criterion when
\varphi
has (almost) linear growth. To achieve this, we need to adapt the above argument.
Indeed, while the
R^{Z}
term satisfies a similar estimate, the term

\|\varphi(Y_{\sigma^{n}})\|\|X\|_{\gamma}t^{\gamma}\sim nt^{\gamma}
in (
1.4
) can no
longer be uniformly bounded without making
(t_{n})
summable.
Instead, we will leverage a different set of contours
(r_{n})
which
grows exponentially. To be more precise, taking
r_{n}\sim 2^{n}
, we have that

r_{n+1}-r_{n}\sim 2^{n}
and thus, the desired estimate is of the form

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:del-Y-est2}\|Y_{(\tau^{{n}}+t)\wedge\tau^{{n+1}}}-Y_{\tau^{n}}\|<\varepsilon 2^{n}

(1.5)

for some small
\varepsilon
independent of
n
. Namely, for this choice of
(r_{n})
,
the term
\|\varphi(Y_{\tau^{n}})\|\|X\|_{\gamma}t^{\gamma}\sim 2^{n}t^{\gamma}
in (
1.5
) is no longer an issue as
one can simply take
t_{n}\sim\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{\gamma}}
which is clearly not summable.

However, one should not yet celebrate as now the
R^{Z}
term becomes problematic as the
estimate there (cf. Lemma
4.11
) would impose that

t_{n}\lesssim 2^{-n}
which is most certainly summable. To remedy this, we introduce
2^{n}
sub-level bands
within each exponential level set of width 1 and track the times at which the solution crosses these bands.
As it turns out, the remainder
R^{Z}
can be controlled on these smaller intervals while cancellation
of terms occurs for the Riemann sum estimate on
R^{Z}
on these intervals. This is the content of
Section
4.3
and Appendix
A
resulting in Theorem
4.12
.

1.2
Notations

We collect here only the conventions used repeatedly throughout the paper and which are not
introduced formally in the preliminaries. For a two-parameter map
A
, we write

\delta A_{st}:=A_{t}-A_{s},

and for an interval
I\subseteq[0,T]
and exponent
\alpha>0
, we use the Hölder semi-norms

\|A\|_{\alpha;I}:=\sup_{s<t\in I}\frac{\|A_{st}\|}{|t-s|^{\alpha}},\qquad\|A\|_{\infty;I}:=\sup_{t\in I}\|A_{t}\|.

As usual,
A\lesssim B
means that
A\leq CB
for a constant
C>0
independent of the relevant variables.

In the non-explosion arguments of Section
4.1
, for
r>0
we write

\tau^{r}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:\|Y_{t}\|\geq r\}
.
Moreover, in Section
4.3
and the appendix, where the argument
is one-dimensional, we instead use

\tilde{\tau}^{r}:=\inf\{t:|Y_{t}|\geq 2r\},\qquad\tilde{\sigma}^{r}:=\sup\{t<\tilde{\tau}^{r}:|Y_{t}|\leq r\}.

We introduce any further proof-local notations at the point of use.

2
Preliminaries

We dedicate this section to a brief self-contained introduction to the setting of branched rough paths. We also
note the works of
[
HK14
,
BCMW22
,
TZ20
,
VRST25
,
BCFP19
]
and of course,
[
Gub06
]

all of which include nice expositions to this theory.

2.1
Rooted Labelled Trees

For higher order rough paths, it is useful to introduce tree notations to keep track of the
algebraic and analytic conditions for the extra terms arising from the Taylor expansion.

Definition 2.1
.

Denote
{\mathcal{T}}
for the set of all rooted and labeled trees and
{\mathcal{F}}
for the set of the associated
forests, i.e.
{\mathcal{F}}
is the free abelian monoid generated by
{\mathcal{T}}
and
f\in{\mathcal{F}}
is a finite
collection of rooted labeled trees (where we allow multiple copies of the same tree).

Notation wise, we use greek letters
\tau,\sigma,\varrho,\dots
for trees in
{\mathcal{T}}
and

f,g,h\dots
for forests in
{\mathcal{F}}
.

Some examples of rooted and labeled trees are

For
\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}
, denote
f_{\tau}
for the number of copies of
\tau
in
f
. Thus, we can write

f=\prod_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}}\tau^{f_{\tau}}

where
f_{\tau}
is zero for all but finitely many terms. Namely,
\tau\in f
if and only if

f_{\tau}\neq 0
. For
\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}
, the order of
\tau
:
|\tau|
is simply the number of vertices of

\tau
and for
f\in{\mathcal{F}}
,
|f|=\sum_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}}f_{\tau}|\tau|
. We also write
\#f=\sum_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}}f_{\tau}
.

We denote
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
for the free vector space generated by
{\mathcal{F}}
so
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}

is a unital commutative algebra with identity
\mathbf{1}
. We define the inner product of
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}

by setting

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:inner-product}{\left\langle f,f^{\prime}\right\rangle}=\mathbf{1}_{f=f^{\prime}}

(2.1)

for all
f,f^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{F}}
and extending linearly.

We define the coproduct
\Delta:{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}\to{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}\otimes{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}

by first defining
\Delta
on
{\mathcal{F}}
inductively and then extending linearly. In particular, we set

•

\Delta\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}\otimes\mathbf{1}
.

•

For
f\in{\mathcal{F}}
,
\Delta f=\prod_{h\in{\mathcal{T}}}(\Delta h)^{f_{h}}
.

•

For
f\in{\mathcal{F}}
,
\Delta[f]_{a}=[f]_{a}\otimes\mathbf{1}+(\text{id}\otimes[-]_{a})\Delta f
.

.

Geometrically, the coproduct of a tree corresponds to the sum of all the ways of splitting the tree
into two parts by a single cut, with the part containing the root placed on the right hand side of the tensor product.
Namely, we have that

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:coproduct-sum-subtrees}\Delta\tau=\tau\otimes\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{1}\otimes\tau+\sum_{\sigma\subsetneq\tau}(\tau\setminus\sigma)\otimes\sigma

(2.2)

where the sum is over all proper subtrees
\sigma
of
\tau
with the same root and

\tau\setminus\sigma
is the rooted tree obtained by removing
\sigma
from
\tau
.

2.2
Hopf Algebra

The algebra
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
equipped with the coproduct
\Delta
forms what is known as a
Hopf algebra (in particular, it is known as the Connes-Kreimer Hopf algebra). We in this section provide an
informal description of this structure.

Before we proceed with defining Hopf algebras, we first need to introduce
bialgebras
.
Suppose we have an algebra
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
acting on another algebra
{\mathcal{H}}
via the action

{\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle}:{\mathcal{H}}^{*}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}\to\mathbb{R}.

Roughly speaking, a bialgebra is then
{\mathcal{H}}
equipped with a
coproduct

\Delta:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}

which encodes this pairing and in particular, preserves the product structure of its
coalgebra

{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
. More precisely,

\Delta
is dual to the product operator
\nabla^{*}
of
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
in the sense that

{\left\langle\nabla^{*}(f\otimes g),h\right\rangle}={\left\langle f\otimes g,\Delta h\right\rangle}

where
\nabla^{*}:{\mathcal{H}}^{*}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}^{*}\to{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
is such that
\nabla^{*}(x,y)=xy
. Thus, in some
sense, once we have the coproduct
\Delta
, we can forget about
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
and work solely with
{\mathcal{H}}
.

A bialgebra
({\mathcal{H}},\Delta)
is
graded
if it has the decomposition

{\mathcal{H}}=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}{\mathcal{H}}_{(n)}

where
{\mathcal{H}}_{(n)}
are vector spaces such that for all
n,m\in\mathbb{N}
,

{\mathcal{H}}_{(n)}\cdot{\mathcal{H}}_{(m)}\subseteq{\mathcal{H}}_{(n+m)},\text{ and }\Delta{\mathcal{H}}_{(n)}\subseteq\bigoplus_{p+q=n}{\mathcal{H}}_{(p)}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}_{(q)}.

Denoting
{\mathcal{F}}_{(n)}=\{f\in{\mathcal{F}}:|f|=n\}
, taking
{\mathcal{H}}_{(n)}={\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}_{(n)}\right\rangle}
,
we observe that
{\mathcal{F}}
is a graded bialgebra.

While the coproduct preserves the product structure of
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
, we would also like a map which
preserves the units (invertible elements) of
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
. This is achieved with the
antipole

map
S:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\mathcal{H}}
which is required to satisfy

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:antipole}\nabla(S\otimes\text{id})\Delta h=\nabla(\text{id}\otimes S)\Delta h={\left\langle\mathbf{1},h\right\rangle}\mathbf{1}

(2.3)

for all
h\in{\mathcal{H}}
, where
\nabla
is the product operator of
{\mathcal{H}}
and

{\left\langle\mathbf{1},h\right\rangle}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }h=\mathbf{1},\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

This condition is motivated by the fact that, if
S
is such that for any unit
f\in{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
,

S^{*}f=f^{-1}
where
S^{*}:{\mathcal{H}}^{*}\to{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
is the dual of
S
, then

{\left\langle f\otimes f,(S\otimes\text{id})\Delta h\right\rangle}={\left\langle\nabla^{*}(S^{*}f\otimes f),h\right\rangle}={\left\langle S^{*}f\cdot f,h\right\rangle}={\left\langle\mathbf{1},h\right\rangle}.

On the other hand, as
f
is a unit,

{\left\langle f\otimes f,{\left\langle\mathbf{1},h\right\rangle}\mathbf{1}\otimes\mathbf{1}\right\rangle}={\left\langle\mathbf{1},h\right\rangle}.

Hence, in order for
S
to preserve the unit structure of
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
, it is necessary to require

\nabla(S\otimes\text{id})\Delta h=\nabla{\left\langle\mathbf{1},h\right\rangle}\mathbf{1}\otimes\mathbf{1}={\left\langle\mathbf{1},h\right\rangle}\mathbf{1}
.

With the antipole motivated, a Hopf algebra is then simply a bialgebra equipped with an antipole.

Proposition 2.2
.

A graded bialgebra satisfying
{\mathcal{H}}_{(0)}=\mathbb{R}
is automatically a Hopf algebra.

Thus, as
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}_{(0)}\right\rangle}=\mathbb{R}
, it follows
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
is a Hopf algebra.
The antipole
S
of
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
can be computed explicitly by using the identity (
2.3
).
We give some examples:

•

S\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}
.

.

Equipping
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
with the inner product as defined by Equation (
2.1
),
we can view
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
acting on itself via the action
{\left\langle f,\cdot\right\rangle}

for all
f\in{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
. Thus, the underlying bialgebra of
({\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle},\Delta,S)

can be viewed as
{\mathcal{H}}={\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
with itself as its own coalgebra
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}={\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}

(with a different multiplication). We now give a description of the algebraic structure of

{\mathcal{H}}^{*}={\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
.

By the property of the coproduct, if
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}={\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
has product
\nabla^{*}(f,g)=f\curvearrowright g
, then
for any
f,g,h\in{\mathcal{F}}
, we have the defining property for
\nabla^{*}
:

{\left\langle f\curvearrowright g,h\right\rangle}={\left\langle\nabla^{*}(f,g),h\right\rangle}={\left\langle f\otimes g,\Delta h\right\rangle}.

The product
\curvearrowright
is known as the
convolution product
(or the graphing operation e.g.
[
BCMW22
]
).
We observe that for
f,g\in{\mathcal{F}}
,

{\left\langle f\curvearrowright g,h\right\rangle}=1
if and only if
f\otimes g
is a term of
\Delta h
. For trees, the
convolution can be described geometrically with

\tau_{1}\curvearrowright\tau_{2}=\tau_{1}\tau_{2}+\tau_{1}\curvearrowright_{t}\tau_{2}

for
\tau_{1},\tau_{2}\in{\mathcal{T}}
where
\tau_{1}\curvearrowright_{t}\tau_{2}
denotes the sum of all trees obtained
by attaching
\tau_{1}
to a vertex of
\tau_{2}
.

On the other hand,
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
equipped with concatenation
\cdot
(i.e. free product defined by
h_{1}\cdot h_{2}=h_{1}h_{2}
)
forms an associative (
non-commutative
) algebra.
We denote its coproduct by
\delta:{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}\to{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}\otimes{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
, i.e. we have that

{\left\langle\delta f,h_{1}\otimes h_{2}\right\rangle}={\left\langle f,h_{1}h_{2}\right\rangle}.

Thus, if
\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}
, then, using Sweedler’s notation,

1={\left\langle\tau,\tau\cdot\mathbf{1}\right\rangle}={\left\langle\delta\tau,\tau\otimes\mathbf{1}\right\rangle}=\sum{\left\langle\tau^{(1)},\tau\right\rangle}{\left\langle\tau^{(2)},\mathbf{1}\right\rangle}.

Namely, there exists a unique component
i
of
\delta\tau
for which
\tau^{(1)i}=\tau
and

\tau^{(2)i}=\mathbf{1}
.

The tensor algebra
T(\mathbb{R}^{d})
can be identified in
{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
by identifying

e_{a}
by
a
,
e_{b}\otimes e_{a}
by
a
b
,
e_{c}\otimes e_{b}\otimes e_{a}
by
c
b
a

and so on for
a,b,c=1,\dots,d
. Namely, denoting

\iota:T(\mathbb{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow{\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}\right\rangle}
for this inclusion,

\iota(T(\mathbb{R}^{d}))
corresponds to the set of all trees with a single branch.

Definition 2.3
.

Let
{\mathcal{H}}
be a Hopf algebra with coalgebra
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
. Denote
\Hom({\mathcal{H}},\mathbb{R})\subseteq{\mathcal{H}}^{*}

for the space of characters (i.e.
\mathbb{R}
-valued algebra homomorphisms) of
{\mathcal{H}}
.

For all (by an abuse of notation)
f={\left\langle f,\cdot\right\rangle}\in\Hom({\mathcal{H}},\mathbb{R})
,
as
f
is multiplicative, it follows that

{\left\langle f,h_{1}h_{2}\right\rangle}={\left\langle f,h_{1}\right\rangle}{\left\langle f,h_{2}\right\rangle}={\left\langle f\otimes f,h_{1}\otimes h_{2}\right\rangle}.

On the other hand, denoting
\delta
for the coproduct on the coalgebra
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
, we have

{\left\langle\delta f,h_{1}\otimes h_{2}\right\rangle}={\left\langle f,h_{1}h_{2}\right\rangle}.

Thus, we can identify elements of
\Hom({\mathcal{H}},\mathbb{R})
with
f\in{\mathcal{H}}^{*}
which satisfies

\delta f=f\otimes f
. More precisely,

\Hom({\mathcal{H}},\mathbb{R})\simeq\{f\in{\mathcal{H}}^{*}:\delta f=f\otimes f\}=:G({\mathcal{H}}).

Definition 2.4
.

G({\mathcal{H}})
forms a group and is known as the
Butcher group
.

Proposition 2.5
.

For all
f\in G({\mathcal{H}})
,
f^{-1}=S^{*}f
with
S^{*}
being the adjoint of the antipole.

2.3
Branched Rough Paths

Finally, we can now define branched rough paths. Defining
{\mathcal{H}}^{*}_{(n)}={\left\langle{\mathcal{F}}_{(n)}\right\rangle}

where the notation
∗
indicates we are working in the dual space, we define

G_{N}({\mathcal{H}})=\frac{G({\mathcal{H}})}{\{f\in G({\mathcal{H}}):{\left\langle f,h\right\rangle}=0\text{ for all }h\in{\mathcal{F}},\ 1\leq|h|\leq N\}}

where the fraction indicates the quotient group (it is not difficult to see that the denominator
is indeed a normal subgroup). Namely, we identify two characters which agree on all forests of order at most
N
. Then, for a path
X=(X^{a})_{a\in I}
, we define the branched
rough paths over
X
by specifying its iterated integrals.

Definition 2.6
.

For a map
\mathbf{X}:[0,T]\to G_{N}({\mathcal{H}})
, we denote
\mathbf{X}_{st}=\mathbf{X}^{-1}_{s}\curvearrowright\mathbf{X}_{t}
.
For any
\gamma\in(\frac{1}{N+1},\frac{1}{N}]
, we say
\mathbf{X}
is a
\gamma
-Hölder branched rough path if

\sup_{s<t\in[0,T]}\frac{|{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},f\right\rangle}|}{|t-s|^{\gamma|f|}}<\infty

for all
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N}
.

For a branched rough path
\mathbf{X}
, we define its path component
X^{a}
by

\gamma
-Hölder branched rough path are
\gamma
-Hölder.
Moreover, Chen’s condition (that is
\mathbf{X}_{st}=\mathbf{X}_{su}\curvearrowright\mathbf{X}_{ut}
) is automatically
satisfied by branched rough paths.

\tau=[f]_{a}
, we interpret
{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},\tau\right\rangle}=\int_{s}^{t}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{sr},f\right\rangle}\differential X^{a}_{r}

and so on. These form a basis should we repeatedly apply Taylor expansion of a solution to an RDE.

Definition 2.7
.

A path
\mathbf{Y}:[0,T]\to{\mathcal{H}}_{N-1}=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{N-1}{\mathcal{H}}_{(n)}
is a

\mathbf{X}
-controlled rough path for some
\gamma
-Hölder branched rough path
\mathbf{X}
if

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:remainder}R^{Y,f}_{st}=R^{f}_{st}={\left\langle f,\mathbf{Y}_{t}\right\rangle}-{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st}\curvearrowright f,\mathbf{Y}_{s}\right\rangle}

(2.4)

satisfies

\sup_{s<t\in[0,T]}\frac{|R^{f}_{st}|}{|t-s|^{(N-|f|)\gamma}}<\infty

for all
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}
. We denote
Y_{t}={\left\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{Y}_{t}\right\rangle}
for the
path component of
\mathbf{Y}
and furthermore, for
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}
, denote

\partial^{f}_{X}Y_{t}={\left\langle f,\mathbf{Y}_{t}\right\rangle}
. We call
\partial^{f}_{X}Y_{t}
the
f
-th Gubinelli
derivative of
\mathbf{Y}
against
\mathbf{X}
.

For simplicity, our discussion from now on focuses to the case where
I=\{1,2,\dots,d\}

and
X=(X^{a})_{a=1}^{d}=({\left\langle\mathbf{X},\mathchoice{\hbox to9.68pt{\vbox to6.58pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 2.33386pt\lower-3.29149pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@roundjoin\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linejoin} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@roundcap\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linecap} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{}{{}}{}

Moreover, we observe that a similar formula holds for other levels of the remainder (Proposition
2.9
).
For the sake of computation, we introduce the following short hands. For all
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N}
,

•

\Delta_{r}f=\Delta f-\mathbf{1}\otimes f
which is known as the reduced coproduct,

•

for
g,h\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N}
, set
c_{r}(f,g,h)={\left\langle g\otimes h,\Delta_{r}f\right\rangle}={\left\langle g\curvearrowright h,f\right\rangle}\mathbf{1}_{g\neq\mathbf{1}}
.
Namely,

\Delta_{r}f=\sum_{g,h\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N}}c_{r}(f,g,h)g\otimes h.

Lemma 2.8
.

For
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N}
,
c_{r}(f,g,h)=\sum_{l}{\left\langle f,l\right\rangle}c_{r}(l,g,h)
.

Proof.

∑_g, h (∑_l ⟨f, l⟩ c_r(l, g, h)) g ⊗h

= ∑_l ⟨f, l⟩ ∑_g, h c_r(l, g, h) g ⊗h

= ∑_l ⟨f, l⟩ Δ_r l

= Δ_r (∑_l ⟨f, l⟩ l) = Δ_r f.

Using these notations, we have the equivalent formulation of the remainder term.

Proposition 2.9
.

For a
\gamma
-Hölder rough path
\mathbf{X}
and a path
\mathbf{Y}:[0,T]\to{\mathcal{H}}^{*}_{N-1}
,
for all
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}
,

R_{st}^{f}=\delta(\partial^{f}_{X}Y)_{st}-\sum_{g,h\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}c_{r}(g,h,f)\partial^{g}_{X}Y_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},h\right\rangle}

where
R^{f}
is defined as in Equation (
2.4
).

Proof.

We compute,

\displaystyle R^{f}_{st}

\displaystyle=\partial^{f}_{X}Y_{t}-{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st}\curvearrowright f,\mathbf{Y}_{s}\right\rangle}=\partial^{f}_{X}Y_{t}-{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st}\otimes f,\Delta\mathbf{Y}_{s}\right\rangle}

\displaystyle=\partial^{f}_{X}Y_{t}-{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st}\otimes f,\mathbf{1}\otimes\mathbf{Y}_{s}\right\rangle}-{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st}\otimes f,\Delta_{r}\mathbf{Y}_{s}\right\rangle}

\displaystyle=\delta(\partial^{f}_{X}Y)_{st}-\sum_{h,l}c_{r}(\mathbf{Y}_{s},h,l){\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st}\otimes f,h\otimes l\right\rangle}

Thus, by applying Lemma
2.8
, it follows that

\displaystyle R^{f}_{st}

\displaystyle=\delta(\partial^{f}_{X}Y)_{st}-\sum_{h,l}\sum_{g}c_{r}(g,h,l)\partial^{g}_{X}Y_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},h\right\rangle}{\left\langle f,l\right\rangle}

\displaystyle=\delta(\partial^{f}_{X}Y)_{st}-\sum_{g,h}c_{r}(g,h,f)\partial^{g}_{X}Y_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},h\right\rangle}

as desired.

Proposition 2.10
.

Let
\mathbf{Y}:[0,T]\to{\mathcal{H}}^{*}_{N-1}
be a controlled rough path against the
\gamma
-Hölder
rough path
\mathbf{X}
. Then, denoting the two parameter process

I_{st}^{a}=\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}\partial^{f}_{X}Y_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},[f]_{a}\right\rangle}

for any
a\in I
, we have that

\|\delta I\|_{(N+1)\gamma}\lesssim\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}\|R^{f}\|_{(N-|f|)\gamma}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},[f]\right\rangle}\|_{(|f|+1)\gamma}.

As a consequence of the above proposition, in the case where
(N+1)\gamma>1
, we may apply the sewing
lemma to
I_{st}
to define the rough integral

\int_{s}^{t}Y_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}={\left(\int_{s}^{t}Y_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}^{a}\right)}_{a=1}^{d}:={\left(\lim_{|{\mathcal{P}}|\to 0}\sum_{(u,v)\in{\mathcal{P}}}I_{uv}^{a}\right)}_{a=1}^{d}

with
{\mathcal{P}}
being a partition of
[s,t]
and we have the remainder inequality

\displaystyle{\left\|\int_{s}^{t}Y_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}-{\left(\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}\partial^{f}_{X}Y_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},[f]_{a}\right\rangle}\right)}_{a=1}^{d}\right\|}

\displaystyle\lesssim{\left(\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}\|R^{f}\|_{(N-|f|)\gamma}\|\mathbf{X}^{[f]}\|_{(|f|+1)\gamma}\right)}|t-s|^{(N+1)\gamma}

We note that at this point
\int_{s}^{\cdot}Y_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}
takes value in
\mathbb{R}^{d}
and is notably not a tree/forest
path. As we would like to talk about rough differential equations, namely we would want to phrase a fixed point
argument involving rough integrals, we need to extend the
\mathbb{R}^{d}
-valued path
\int_{s}^{\cdot}Y_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}

to a forest path
\int_{s}^{\cdot}\mathbf{Y}_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}
. This is achieved by specifying

\partial^{f}_{X}{\left(\int_{s}^{\cdot}\mathbf{Y}_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}\right)}={\left\langle f,\int_{s}^{\cdot}\mathbf{Y}_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}\right\rangle}

for each
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}^{*}
with

1.

\partial^{\mathbf{1}}_{X}\int_{s}^{\cdot}\mathbf{Y}_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}=\int_{s}^{\cdot}Y_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}
.

2.

For
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{\leq N-2}
, we set
\partial^{[f]}_{X}\int_{0}^{\cdot}\mathbf{Y}_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}=\partial^{f}_{X}\mathbf{Y}_{\cdot}
.

3.

For
f_{1}\cdot f_{2}\in{\mathcal{F}}_{\leq N-1}
,
\partial^{f_{1}\cdot f_{2}}_{X}\int_{0}^{\cdot}\mathbf{Y}_{r}\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}=0
.

Thus, with the context of the construction
2
and rough differential equations in mind, we
observe that if
\mathbf{Y}
is a solution to the rough differential equation

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:bRDE}\differential\mathbf{Y}_{t}=b(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\differential t+\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\differential\mathbf{X}_{t},

(2.5)

\mathbf{Y}
necessarily satisfies the algebraic condition that

\partial^{[f]}_{X}Y=\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})
. This motivates the following definition.

Definition 2.11
(Coherence).

A
\mathbf{X}
-controlled rough path
\mathbf{Y}
is said to be
\varphi
-coherent if for all

f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-2}
,

\partial^{[f]}_{X}Y=\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}).

3
A priori estimates for coherent controlled rough paths

Throughout this section, we fix
\mathbf{X}
to be a level
N
branched rough path on
\mathbb{R}^{d}

and take
\mathbf{Y}
to be a
\varphi
-coherent
\mathbf{X}
-controlled rough path on
\mathbb{R}^{m}

for some function
\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to{\mathcal{L}}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbb{R}^{m})
.

3.1
Composition with smooth functions

It is well known that (cf.
[
FH20
, Section 7.3]
), in the case where
N=2
, the
composition of controlled rough paths with a smooth function is again a controlled rough path. More precisely, for

(X,\mathbb{X})\in{\mathcal{C}}^{\gamma}([0,T],V)
,
(Y,Y^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{D}}_{X}^{2\gamma}([0,T],W)
and

\varphi\in C^{2}(W,\bar{W})
, we have that

(\varphi(Y),\varphi(Y)^{\prime})=(\varphi(Y),D\varphi(Y)Y^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{D}}_{X}^{2\gamma}([0,T],\bar{W}).

This fact can be generalized for branched rough paths resulting in the following.

Proposition 3.1
(Lemma 8.6 of
[
Gub06
]
).

For any
\varphi\in C^{N}
, defining
\varphi(\mathbf{Y})
by

\varphi(\mathbf{Y})=\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})f

where

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:deriv-comp-def}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})=\sum_{\tau_{1}\cdots\tau_{\#f}=f}\frac{1}{(\#f)!}D^{\#f}\varphi(Y)[(\partial^{\tau_{i}}_{X}Y)_{i=1}^{\#f}]

(3.1)

for any
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}
, we have that
\varphi(\mathbf{Y})
is
also a controlled rough path against
\mathbf{X}
.

As we had assumed that
\mathbf{Y}
is
\varphi
-coherent, Equation (
3.1
)
can be iterated as in the following example so that
\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})
can be
written explicitly as a function
\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi
of
Y
.

We introduce the following combinatorial factor
\Pi:{\mathcal{F}}\to\mathbb{N}
where
\Pi(\mathbf{1})=1
,
and for any
f\in{\mathcal{F}}

\Pi([f])=\Pi(f)=\prod_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}}f_{\tau}!\Pi(\tau)^{f_{\tau}}.

\Pi(f)
is known as the symmetry factor of
f
. Geometrically, for
\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}
,
\Pi(\tau)

is the number of permutations one can do on the branches starting from any
vertices of
\tau
without changing the tree. E.g. if

The symmetric factor allows us to easily compute the coefficient on the right hand
side of (
3.1
). In particular, by noticing that the multinomial coefficient can be
written as

\mul(f)=\sum_{\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{\#f}\in{\mathcal{T}}_{N-1}}\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau_{1}\cdots\tau_{\#f}=f\}}=\binom{\#f}{f_{h}:h\in f}=\frac{(\#f)!}{\Pi(f)}\prod_{\tau\in f}\Pi(\tau),

it follows that

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:deriv-comp-alt}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})=\prod_{\tau\in f}\frac{\Pi(\tau)}{\Pi(f)}D^{\#f}\varphi(Y)[(\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y)_{\tau\in f}].

(3.2)

In the level
N=2
case, we recall that we have the Taylor estimate

\begin{split}\|R^{\varphi(\mathbf{Y})}_{st}\|\leq&\sup_{\lambda\in[0,1]}\frac{1}{2}\|D^{2}\varphi((1-\lambda)Y_{s}+\lambda Y_{t})\|\|Y_{st}\|^{2}+\|D\varphi(Y_{s})R^{\mathbf{Y}}_{st}\|,\end{split}

(3.3)

For a general level
N

\tau=\mathbf{1}
:

Proposition 3.4
.

Taking
\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}
as above, we have

R^{\varphi(\mathbf{Y}),\mathbf{1}}_{st}=\delta(\varphi(Y))_{st}-\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\frac{1}{k!}D^{k}\varphi(Y_{s})[(\delta Y_{st})^{\otimes k}]-R^{\sharp}_{st}

where

R^{\sharp}_{st}:=\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\sum_{m=1}^{k}\frac{(-1)^{m}}{k!}\binom{k}{m}D^{k}\varphi(Y_{s}){\left[(R^{\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{1}}_{st})^{\otimes m}\otimes(\delta Y_{st})^{\otimes(k-m)}\right]},

which has Hölder regularity
N\gamma
.

Proof.

Observing, for any
f,g\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}\setminus\{\mathbf{1}\}=:{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}^{+}
, we have that

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:crone}c_{r}(f,g,\mathbf{1})={\left\langle f,g\right\rangle}.

(3.4)

Thus, by Proposition
2.9
and the fact that
\partial^{f}_{X}Y=0

for all
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}^{+}\setminus{\mathcal{T}}_{N-1}
,

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:remain-Y-one}\delta Y_{st}-R^{\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{1}}_{st}=\sum_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}_{N-1}^{+}}\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},\tau\right\rangle}.

(3.5)

Hence, (setting
\partial^{f}_{X}Y=0
for all
f\in{\mathcal{F}}
with
|f|\geq N
) we observe that

\displaystyle\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}^{+}_{N-1}}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{s}){\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},f\right\rangle}=

\displaystyle\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}^{+}_{N-1}}\sum_{\tau_{1}\cdots\tau_{\#f}=f}\frac{1}{(\#f)!}D^{\#f}\varphi(Y_{s}){\left[\bigotimes^{\#f}_{i=1}\partial^{\tau_{i}}_{X}Y_{s}\right]}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},f\right\rangle}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\frac{1}{k!}D^{k}\varphi(Y_{s}){\left[{\left(\sum_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}^{+}_{N-1}}\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},\tau\right\rangle}\right)}^{\otimes k}\right]}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\frac{1}{k!}D^{k}\varphi(Y_{s}){\left[(\delta Y_{st}-R^{\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{1}}_{st})^{\otimes k}\right]}.

where the first equality is due to Proposition
3.1
. Thus,

The higher order remainder terms (i.e.

Lemma 3.5
.

For any
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}
, we have that

R^{\varphi(\mathbf{Y}),f}_{st}=\delta(\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}))_{st}-\sum_{k=1}^{N-|f|-1}\frac{1}{k!}D^{k}[\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{s})]{\left[{\left(\sum_{1\leq|\tau|\leq N-k}\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},\tau\right\rangle}\right)}^{\otimes k}\right]}.

Thus, as a direct consequence of Equation (
3.5
), we have the following Taylor
expansion for higher order remainders.

Corollary 3.6
.

For any
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}
, we have that

R^{\varphi(\mathbf{Y}),f}_{st}=\delta(\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}))_{st}-\sum_{k=1}^{N-|f|-1}\frac{1}{k!}D^{k}[\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{s})]{\left[(\delta Y_{st})^{\otimes k}\right]}-R^{\sharp,f}_{st}

where

has regularity
\geq N\gamma

More precisely,

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:R-sharp-def}R^{\sharp,f}_{st}=\sum_{k=1}^{N-|f|-1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}=k\\
m_{1}\neq k\end{subarray}}\frac{(-1)^{m_{2}+m_{3}}}{k!}\binom{k}{m_{1},m_{2},m_{3}}D^{k}[\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{s})][A_{st}^{m_{1},m_{2},m_{3}}],

(3.6)

for which the
m_{1},m_{2}
and
m_{3}
are summed over the non-negative integers and

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:A-def}A_{st}^{m_{1},m_{2},m_{3}}:=(\delta Y_{st})^{\otimes m_{1}}\otimes(R^{\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{1}}_{st})^{\otimes m_{2}}\otimes{\left(\sum_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}_{N-1}\setminus{\mathcal{T}}_{N-k}}\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},\tau\right\rangle}\right)}^{\otimes m_{3}}.

(3.7)

Lemma 3.7
.

For any
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}
, we have the estimate

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:remain-phi-Y}\begin{split}&\ \|R^{\varphi(\mathbf{Y}),f}\|_{(N-|f|)\gamma}\\
\lesssim\ &\|R^{\sharp,f}\|_{N\gamma}|t-s|^{|f|\gamma}+\frac{|{\mathcal{T}}_{N-1}|^{N-|f|-1}}{(N-|f|)!}C_{[s,t]}^{f}\|R^{\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{1}}\|_{N\gamma}^{N-|f|}|t-s|^{(N-1)(N-|f|)\gamma}\\
&+\frac{|{\mathcal{T}}_{N-1}|^{N-|f|-1}}{(N-|f|)!}C_{[s,t]}^{f}\sum_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}^{+}_{N-1}}(\|\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y\|_{\infty;[s,t]}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},\tau\right\rangle}\|_{|\tau|\gamma}|t-s|^{(|\tau|-1)\gamma})^{(N-|f|)}.\end{split}

(3.8)

where for any
I\subseteq\mathbb{R}
, we have denoted

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:Cf-def}C_{I}^{f}:=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}u<v\in I\\
\lambda\in[0,1]\end{subarray}}\|D^{N-|f|}[\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\lambda\mathbf{Y}_{u}+(1-\lambda)\mathbf{Y}_{v})]\|.

(3.9)

Proof.

Applying the Taylor theorem to Corollary
3.6
, we have that

\displaystyle\|R^{\varphi(\mathbf{Y}),f}\|_{(N-|f|)\gamma}\leq

\displaystyle\frac{C_{[s,t]}^{f}}{(N-|f|)!}\|Y\|_{\gamma}^{N-|f|}+\|R^{\sharp,f}\|_{N\gamma}|t-s|^{|f|\gamma}

Thus, we obtain the desired inequality as

\|Y\|_{\gamma}\leq\|R^{\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{1}}\|_{N\gamma}|t-s|^{(N-1)\gamma}+\sum_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}^{+}_{N-1}}\|\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y\|_{\infty;[s,t]}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},\tau\right\rangle}\|_{|\tau|\gamma}|t-s|^{(|\tau|-1)\gamma}

which follows by Equation (
3.5
).

3.2
An a priori estimate of the derivative

As we will need to control the coefficient arising from the Taylor estimate of Lemma
3.7
,
we will in this section establish a useful bound on the derivatives
\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})

in terms of estimates on
\varphi
and its derivatives.

Definition 3.8
.

For
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N}
and
k\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}
, we define
\Lambda_{k}(f)
inductively by

\Lambda_{k}(\mathbf{1})=0
, and

\Lambda_{k}([f])=\mathbf{1}_{\#f=k}+\Lambda_{k}(f)=\mathbf{1}_{\#f=k}+\sum_{\tau\in f}\Lambda_{k}(\tau).

Namely, for any
k
,
\Lambda_{k}(f)
counts the number of vertices in
f
with exactly
k
children.

Lemma 3.9
.

For all
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N}
and constant
\beta
, we have that

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:sum-Lambda-eq}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{k}(f)(1-\beta k)=(1-\beta)|f|+\beta\#f.

(3.10)

Proof.

It suffices to show
\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{k}(f)(1-k)=\#f
since if this were the case,

\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{k}(f)(1-\beta k)=(1-\beta)\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{k}(f)+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{k}(f)(1-k)=(1-\beta)|f|+\beta\#f

as desired.

For this, we prove by induction on
f\in{\mathcal{T}}_{N}
. The equality is
clear for the base case
f=\mathbf{1}
. Thus, taking
f=\prod_{i=1}^{m}[h_{i}]
and assuming (
3.10
)
for each
[h_{i}]
, it remains to show (
3.10
) for
[f]
. Indeed, this is the case as

\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{k}([f])(1-k)

\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}{\left(\mathbf{1}_{k=m}+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\Lambda_{k}([h_{i}])\right)}(1-k)

\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathbf{1}_{k=m}(1-k)+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\Lambda_{k}([h_{i}])(1-k)=(1-m)+m=1.

Thus, for a general forest
f
, we have

\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{k}(f)(1-k)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\sum_{\tau\in f}\Lambda_{k}(\tau)(1-k)=\#f

as claimed.

We remark that, rather than the induction argument as presented above, the equality

\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{k}(f)(1-k)=\#f
alternatively follows by Euler’s formula for planar graphs,
namely,
|\tau|-|E(\tau)|=1
for any tree
\tau
with
E(\tau)
being the set of edges in
\tau
.

Lemma 3.10
.

Assuming
\varphi
is such that
\|D^{k}\varphi(x)\|\leq l(\|x\|)^{\alpha_{k}}
for all
k=0,1,\dots,N
,
we have for any
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}
,

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:partial-bound2}\|\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\|=\|\partial^{[f]}_{X}Y_{t}\|\leq\frac{1}{\Pi(f)}l(\|Y_{t}\|)^{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{k}([f])\alpha_{k}}.

(3.11)

Moreover, if
\alpha_{k}=(1-\beta k)\alpha
for some constants
\alpha
and
\beta
, then

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:pb2-deriv}\|D^{n}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\|\leq\frac{(1+|f|)^{n}}{\Pi(f)}l(\|Y_{t}\|)^{((1+|f|)-(n+|f|)\beta)\alpha}

(3.12)

for any
n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}
,
n\leq N-|f|
.

Proof.

We will first show (
3.11
) by inducting on
f
.
Clearly, the estimate holds for

f=\mathbf{1}
and so, taking
f=\prod_{i=1}^{k}[h_{i}]\in{\mathcal{F}}^{+}_{N-1}
, it suffices to show that
(
3.11
) holds for
f
assuming that it holds for each
h_{i}
. Indeed, we compute

\displaystyle\|\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\|

\displaystyle={\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\Pi(h_{i})}{\Pi(f)}\right)}\|D^{k}\varphi(Y_{t})[(\partial^{h_{i}}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t}))_{i=1}^{k}]\|

\displaystyle\leq{\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\Pi(h_{i})}{\Pi(f)}\right)}l(\|Y_{t}\|)^{\alpha_{k}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{\Pi(h_{i})}l(\|Y_{t}\|)^{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{j}([h_{i}])\alpha_{j}}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Pi(f)}l(\|Y_{t}\|)^{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{j}([f])\alpha_{j}}

as required.

Now, assuming
\alpha_{k}=(1-\beta k)\alpha
, we show

\|D^{n}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\|\leq\frac{(1+|f|)^{n}}{\Pi(f)}l(\|Y_{t}\|)^{-\alpha\beta n+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{j}([f])\alpha_{j}}

(3.13)

from which we obtain the desired estimate by Lemma
3.9
.
For this, we induct on
n
.
The base case
n=0
is precisely
(
3.11
) and thus, it suffices to consider
n\geq 1
assuming the relevant inductive
hypothesis. Again, the estimate is trivial for
f=\mathbf{1}
and so, we may take

f=\prod_{i=1}^{k}[h_{i}]\in{\mathcal{F}}^{+}_{N-1}
. We observe

\displaystyle\|D^{n}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\|={\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\Pi(h_{i})}{\Pi(f)}\right)}{\left\|D^{n}{\left[D^{k}\varphi(Y_{t})[(\partial^{h_{i}}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t}))_{i=1}^{k}]\right]}\right\|}

\displaystyle\leq\

\displaystyle{\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\Pi(h_{i})}{\Pi(f)}\right)}\sum_{m_{0}+\cdots+m_{k}=n}\binom{n}{m_{0},\dots,m_{k}}\|D^{k+m_{0}}\varphi(Y_{t})\|\prod_{i=1}^{k}\|D^{m_{i}}\partial^{h_{i}}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\|

\displaystyle\leq\

\displaystyle{\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\Pi(h_{i})}{\Pi(f)}\right)}\sum_{m_{0}+\cdots+m_{k}=n}\binom{n}{m_{0},\dots,m_{k}}l(\|Y_{t}\|)^{(1-\beta(k+m_{0}))\alpha}

\displaystyle\hskip 113.81102pt\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{(1+|h_{i}|)^{m_{i}}}{\Pi(h_{i})}l(\|Y_{t}\|)^{-\alpha\beta m_{i}+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{j}([h_{i}])\alpha_{j}}

\displaystyle=\

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\Pi(f)}\sum_{m_{0}+\cdots+m_{k}=n}\binom{n}{m_{0},\dots,m_{k}}\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1+|h_{i}|)^{m_{i}}

\displaystyle\hskip 113.81102ptl(\|Y_{t}\|)^{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}{\left(\mathbf{1}_{j=k}+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\Lambda_{j}([h_{i}])\right)}\alpha_{j}-\alpha\beta\sum_{i=0}^{k}m_{i}}

\displaystyle=\

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\Pi(f)}l(\|Y_{t}\|)^{-\alpha\beta n+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\Lambda_{j}([f])\alpha_{j}}{\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{k}(1+|h_{i}|)\right)}^{n}

where we had used the inductive hypothesis to arrive at the third line. Thus, we arrive at the
desired inequality by observing that

\sum_{i=1}^{k}(1+|h_{i}|)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}|[h_{i}]|=|f|
.

4
Non-explosion of branched RDEs

4.1
Branched RDEs with drift and unbounded derivatives

From this point forward, we consider branched RDEs with drift of the form

\differential\mathbf{Y}_{t}=b(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\differential t+\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{t})\differential\mathbf{X}_{t}.

(4.1)

Here
b(\mathbf{Y}_{t}):=b(Y_{t})
and we denote the rough integral

\int_{0}^{t}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{s})\differential\mathbf{X}_{s}=:\mathbf{Z}_{t}
which is also a controlled rough path
against
\mathbf{X}
. More precisely, an
\mathbf{X}
-controlled rough path

\mathbf{Y}:[0,T]\to{\mathcal{H}}_{N-1}
is said to be a solution of the branched RDE (
2.5
) if

•

\partial^{\mathbf{1}}_{X}\mathbf{Y}_{t}=Y_{t}=Y_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}b(Y_{s})\differential s+\int_{0}^{t}\varphi(Y_{s})\differential\mathbf{X}_{s}
,

•

and for all
f\in{\mathcal{F}}^{+}_{N-1}
,
\partial^{f}_{X}\mathbf{Y}_{t}=\partial^{f}_{X}\mathbf{Z}_{t}
.

As remarked before,
\mathbf{Y}
is automatically
\varphi
-coherent and moreover,

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:remain-Y-one-Z}R^{\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{1}}_{st}=R^{\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{1}}_{st}+B^{\sharp}_{st}

(4.2)

where we denote
B^{\sharp}_{st}:=\int_{s}^{t}b(\mathbf{Y}_{r})\differential r
. Moreover, by the sewing lemma,
we have the following estimate for
R^{\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{1}}
.

Lemma 4.1
.

Denoting
\mathbf{Z}
as above, we have

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:remain-Z-one}\begin{split}\|R^{\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{1}}\|_{N\gamma;[s,t]}\lesssim&\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},[f]\right\rangle}\|_{(|f|+1)\gamma}|t-s|^{\gamma}\bigg(\|R^{\sharp,f}\|_{N\gamma;[s,t]}|t-s|^{|f|\gamma}\\
&\hskip 28.45274pt+C_{[s,t]}^{f}{\left(\|R^{\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{1}}\|_{N\gamma;[s,t]}^{N-|f|}+\|B^{\sharp}\|_{N\gamma;[s,t]}^{N-|f|}\right)}|t-s|^{(N-1)(N-|f|)\gamma}\\
&\hskip 28.45274pt+C_{[s,t]}^{f}\sum_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}^{+}_{N-1}}{\left(\|\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y\|_{\infty;[s,t]}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},\tau\right\rangle}\|_{|\tau|\gamma}|t-s|^{(|\tau|-1)\gamma}\right)}^{(N-|f|)}\bigg)\\
&+\sum_{|f|=N-1}\|\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})\|_{\infty;[s,t]}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},[f]\right\rangle}\|_{N\gamma}.\end{split}

(4.3)

Proof.

Since
\partial^{f}_{X}Z=0
for all
\#f\geq 2
, we have that

\displaystyle R^{\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{1}}_{st}

\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{r})\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}-\sum_{\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}_{N-1}^{+}}\partial^{\tau}_{X}Z_{s}{\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},\tau\right\rangle}

\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{r})\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}-\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-2}}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{s}){\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},[f]\right\rangle}.

Consequently, by the estimate from the sewing lemma
2.10
, we obtain

\displaystyle\|R^{\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{1}}_{st}\|\leq\

\displaystyle{\left\|\int_{s}^{t}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{r})\differential\mathbf{X}_{r}-\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{s}){\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},[f]\right\rangle}\right\|}+{\left\|\sum_{|f|=N-1}\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y}_{s}){\left\langle\mathbf{X}_{st},[f]\right\rangle}\right\|}

\displaystyle\lesssim\

\displaystyle|t-s|^{(N+1)\gamma}\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}\|R^{\varphi(\mathbf{Y}),f}\|_{(N-|f|)\gamma;[s,t]}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},[f]\right\rangle}\|_{(|f|+1)\gamma}

\displaystyle+|t-s|^{N\gamma}\sum_{|f|=N-1}\|\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})\|_{\infty;[s,t]}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},[f]\right\rangle}\|_{N\gamma}.

Thus, dividing both sides by
|t-s|^{N\gamma}
, we obtain

\displaystyle\|R^{\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{1}}\|_{N\gamma;[s,t]}\lesssim\

\displaystyle|t-s|^{\gamma}\sum_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}}\|R^{\varphi(\mathbf{Y}),f}\|_{(N-|f|)\gamma;[s,t]}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},[f]\right\rangle}\|_{(|f|+1)\gamma}

\displaystyle+\sum_{|f|=N-1}\|\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})\|_{\infty;[s,t]}\|{\left\langle\mathbf{X},[f]\right\rangle}\|_{N\gamma}.

Finally, by estimating
\|R^{\varphi(\mathbf{Y}),f}\|_{(N-|f|)\gamma;[s,t]}
by Equation (
3.8
),
we obtain the desired result.

For the remainder of this section, we impose the following growth assumption on the coefficients of the branched RDE.

Assumption 4.2
.

Assume that
b
and
\varphi
are such that for all
x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
,

(R.1)

\|b(x)\|\leq l(\|x\|)^{1+\kappa\gamma}
,

(R.2)

\|D^{n}\varphi(x)\|\leq l(\|x\|)^{(\theta-n\kappa)\gamma}
for
n=0,\dots,N

for some non-decreasing function
l:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}_{+}
,
\theta\in[0,1)
and
\kappa\in[0,\frac{1}{N})
.

For all intents and purposes, one may think of
l(r)=c(1+r)
for some
c>0
. However, as this
is not necessary for most of the a priori estimates, we keep the more general form of
l
within this assumption.
We also note that for non-explosion, we will require that
b
satisfies a growth condition of the form

{\left\langle b(x),x\right\rangle}\leq c(1+\|x\|^{2})
for some
c>0
. This assumption is unsurprising as it is necessary
even for the case of ODEs.

For all
r>0
, we recall that we denote
\tau^{r}=\inf\{t\geq 0:\|Y_{t}\|\geq r\}
. Moreover,
let us define

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:BR}B_{r}=\{t\in[0,T]:\|Y_{t}\|\leq r\}

(4.4)

and
I=I^{k,R}_{\leq\varepsilon}
for some interval of length less than or equal to
\varepsilon
and
contained in
B_{R(k+1)}
for some
k\in\mathbb{N},\varepsilon,R>0
to be specified
(in particular, we will specialize

I=[\tau^{Rk},(\tau^{Rk}+\varepsilon)\wedge\tau^{R(k+1)}]
in the proof of Theorem
4.7
).
As a direct consequence of Lemma
3.10
, we have the following estimate.

Corollary 4.3
.

Suppose that
(R.2)
holds for all
n=0,\dots,N
. For all
n+|f|\leq N
, we have that

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:deriv-partial}\|D^{n}[\partial^{f}_{X}\varphi(\mathbf{Y})]\|_{\infty;B_{r}}\lesssim l(r)^{((|f|+1)\theta-(|f|+n)\kappa)\gamma}.

(4.5)

Consequently,
C_{I}^{f}\lesssim l(R(k+1))^{((|f|+1)\theta-N\kappa)\gamma}

and for all
\tau\in{\mathcal{T}}^{+}_{N-1}
,

\|\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y\|_{\infty;I}\lesssim l(R(k+1))^{(|\tau|\theta-(|\tau|-1)\kappa)\gamma}.

Proof.

Equation (
4.5
) follows directly from Lemma
3.10
in which we took

\alpha=\theta\gamma
and
\beta=\frac{\kappa}{\theta}
.

We now proceed to estimate the term
\|R^{\sharp,f}\|_{N\gamma;[s,t]}|t-s|^{(|f|+1)\gamma}

arising in Lemma
4.1
.

Lemma 4.4
.

Assuming Assumption
4.2
and setting

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:h-def}h(\varepsilon):=\varepsilon^{(N-1+\theta)\gamma}\|R^{\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{1}}\|_{N\gamma;I^{k,R}_{\leq\varepsilon}},

(4.6)

we have for all
\varepsilon\leq l(R(k+1))^{-1}\wedge 1
,

\displaystyle\varepsilon^{(N-1+\theta)\gamma}\varepsilon^{(|f|+1)\gamma}\|R^{\sharp,f}\|_{N\gamma;I}\lesssim\sum_{k=0}^{N-|f|-1}\varepsilon^{(1-\theta+\kappa)k\gamma}h(\varepsilon)^{k}.

Proof.

We estimate each summand appearing in
\|R^{\sharp,f}\|_{N\gamma;I}\varepsilon^{(|f|+1)\gamma}
.
Fixing
f\in{\mathcal{F}}_{N-1}
,
k\in\{1,\dots,N-|f|-1\}
,
m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}=k
and
m_{1}\neq k
,
let us denote
A^{m_{1},m_{2},m_{3}}
as in Equation (
3.7
). Then, by Corollary
4.3
,
and Equation (
3.5
), we have that

∥D^k[∂^f_X
φ
(Y)]∥_∞; I ∥A^m_1, m_2, m_3∥_N
γ
; I

≲

∥R^
Y
,
1
∥_N
γ
; I^m_1 + m_2
∑_|
τ
| > N - k
∥∂^
τ
_X Y∥_∞; I^m_3

ε
^(- (|f| + 1)
θ
+ (|f| + k)
κ
+ N(m_1 + m_2 - 1) + |
τ
|m_3)
γ

+

∥R^
Y
,
1
∥_N
γ
; I^m_2
∑_

|
τ
| > N - k

σ
∈
T
_N - 1^+

∥∂_X^
σ
Y∥^m_1_∞; I∥∂_X^
τ
Y∥^m_3_∞; I

ε
^(- (|f| + 1)
θ
+ (|f| + k)

+ N (m_2 - 1) + |
σ
| m_1 + |
τ
| m_3)
γ

in which we have absorbed the terms involving the Hölder norms of
\mathbf{X}
into the constant
indicated by
\lesssim
. We estimate each term individually. By Corollary
4.3

and the fact that
k-m_{3}=m_{1}+m_{2}
, we find

\displaystyle\varepsilon^{(|f|+1)\gamma}\sum_{|\tau|>N-k}\|\partial^{\tau}_{X}Y\|_{\infty;I}^{m_{3}}\varepsilon^{(-(|f|+1)\theta+(|f|+k)\kappa)\gamma}\varepsilon^{N(m_{1}+m_{2}-1)\gamma}\varepsilon^{|\tau|m_{3}\gamma}

\displaystyle\lesssim\

\displaystyle\sum_{|\tau|>N-k}\varepsilon^{((1-\theta)(1+|f|+|\tau|m_{3})+\kappa(|f|+|\tau|m_{3}+m_{1}+m_{2})+N(m_{1}+m_{2}-1))\gamma}

\displaystyle\lesssim\

\displaystyle\varepsilon^{((1-\theta)(1+|f|)+\kappa(|f|+m_{1}+m_{2})+N(m_{1}+m_{2}-1))\gamma}.

Similarly, we have

\displaystyle\varepsilon^{(|f|+1)\gamma}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\tau|>N-k\\

\displaystyle\lesssim\

\displaystyle\varepsilon^{((1-\theta)(1+|f|)+\kappa(|f|+m_{2})+N(m_{2}-1))\gamma}.

Now by Equation (
3.5
),

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:R-Y-one-bd}\|R^{\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{1}}\|_{N\gamma;I}^{p}\lesssim\|R^{\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{1}}\|_{N\gamma;I}^{p}+\|B^{\sharp}\|_{N\gamma;I}^{p}

(4.7)

for any

. Thus, by substituting this into Equation (
), we can estimate the terms of

) involving
\|B^{\sharp}\|_{N\gamma;I}
.
Since by assumption

,

\addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:B-sharp-reg}\|B^{\sharp}\|_{N\gamma;I}\leq\sup_{u<v\in I}\frac{1}{|u-v|^{N\gamma}}\int_{u}^{v}\|b(\mathbf{Y}_{r})\|\differential r\leq\varepsilon^{1-N\gamma}l(R(k+1))^{1+\kappa\gamma}\leq\varepsilon^{-(N+\kappa)\gamma}.

Hence, as

\displaystyle\|B^{\sharp}\|_{N\gamma;I}^{m_{1}+m_{2}}\varepsilon^{((1-\theta)(1+|f|)+\kappa(|f|+m_{1}+m_{2})+N(m_{1}+m_{2}-1))\gamma}\lesssim\varepsilon^{((1-\theta)(1+|f|)+\kappa|f|-N)\gamma},

\displaystyle\|B^{\sharp}\|_{N\gamma;I}^{m_{2}}\varepsilon^{((1-\theta)(1+|f|)+\kappa(|f|+m_{2})+N(m_{2}-1))\gamma}\lesssim\varepsilon^{((1-\theta)(1+|f|)+\kappa|f|-N)\gamma},

by substituting the above estimates into Equation (

\displaystyle\varepsilon^{((N-1)+\theta)\gamma}\varepsilon^{(|f|+1)\gamma}\|R^{\sharp,f}\|_{N\gamma;I}
